title: Data Types — Overview
description: Learn about SQL Server data types including numeric, character string, binary string, date & time, and other data types.

data.text: In SQL Server, a column, variable, and parameter holds a value associated with a type, known as a data type. A data type is an attribute that specifies the type of data that these objects can store — such as integers, character strings, monetary values, date and time, and more.

data.alt: SQL Server data types system overview

data.text: Exact numeric data types store exact numbers such as integers, decimals, or monetary amounts.
For new applications, use time, date, datetime2, and datetimeoffset data types as they align with the SQL Standard and are more portable.

data.title: Note
data.text: SQL Server will remove ntext, text, and image data types in future versions. Use nvarchar(max), varchar(max), and varbinary(max) instead.
Choosing a Data Type in Practice

Data types are not just storage details — they decide what values are legal, how much space a row takes, and which comparisons and indexes stay efficient. The script below stores the same numbers in different types and shows how the type of an operand changes the result.

data.title: Same values, different types, different results
data.content: Integer division truncates, decimal division keeps precision, and the metadata query confirms the declared type of an existing column.
data.code:
DECLARE @a INT = 7, @b INT = 2;

SELECT
    @a / @b                                       AS int_division,      -- 3
    CAST(@a AS DECIMAL(10,2)) / @b                AS decimal_division,  -- 3.500000
    CAST(@a AS FLOAT) / @b                        AS float_division,    -- 3.5
    CAST(@a AS DECIMAL(10,2)) / CAST(@b AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS same_type; -- 3.500000

-- Inspect the declared types of an existing table
SELECT
    c.name          AS column_name,
    t.name          AS data_type,
    c.max_length,
    c.precision,
    c.scale,
    c.is_nullable
FROM sys.columns AS c
JOIN sys.types   AS t ON t.user_type_id = c.user_type_id
WHERE c.object_id = OBJECT_ID('sales.orders');

data.title: The one rule that matters
data.text: Pick the narrowest type that still fits every value the column will ever hold — narrow types make rows smaller, so more rows fit on an 8 KB page and fewer reads are needed. But never pick a type you might have to widen later: changing the type of an indexed column usually forces a rebuild of the table and every affected index.

data.title: Interview answer
data.text: If asked which type to use for money, say `DECIMAL(p, s)` (or the legacy `MONEY`, fixed at 4 decimal places). Never use `FLOAT`/`REAL` for money: binary floating point cannot represent values such as 0.10 exactly, so rounding errors accumulate in totals.

data.title: Data Types Overview Key Points
points: SQL Server provides exact numeric, approximate numeric, date/time, character, Unicode, binary, and other data types.
Use the smallest integer type that can reliably contain all possible values.
For new applications, prefer datetime2, date, time, and datetimeoffset over datetime.
Avoid ntext, text, and image — use their max variants instead.
